content_voiceover: This is the International Classification of Retinoblastoma, or ICRB, which fellows should know cold because it drives treatment choice. Group A is the smallest tumor, three millimeters or less. Group B is a larger tumor, or one located near the macula or the optic disc, or one with a small amount of clear subretinal fluid. Group C adds focal seeds, either subretinal or vitreous, still close to the tumor. Groups B and C together are sometimes remembered with the mnemonic SOAI, and these tumors, along with group A, are generally managed with systemic chemotherapy aimed at globe salvage. Group D means diffuse seeding, subretinal or vitreous seeds spread more than three millimeters from the tumor. Group E is extensive disease, occupying more than half the globe, with neovascular glaucoma, opaque media from hemorrhage, or invasion of the optic nerve, choroid, sclera, or anterior chamber. Group E eyes usually cannot be saved and go to enucleation.
keypoints: Group A, small tumor three millimeters or less
Groups B and C, larger or juxtapapillary tumor with focal seeds, treat with systemic chemotherapy
Group D, diffuse subretinal or vitreous seeding
Group E, extensive disease occupying over half the globe, needs enucleation
keypoint_voiceover: Remember it as a spectrum. Group A is tiny and easy. Groups B and C are bigger or awkwardly located but still salvageable with systemic chemotherapy, sometimes grouped together as SOAI. Group D means the seeding has spread diffusely. And Group E is the eye you cannot save, because of glaucoma, hemorrhage, or invasion beyond the retina, so it goes straight to enucleation.
